reasoning: Both attempts made the same code change and reached the same verdicts on all six items, so the write-ups decide it. B quantifies the load more fully: per-player bandwidth compared with a budget, and server frame time. It also states an explicit rule of measuring before optimizing, flags block count as the real long-term risk, and shows the lookup change keeps behavior identical even for hostile input. A has one point B lacks: the client's `IsA` assert would fail under item 3. That is good, but it doesn't outweigh B's more thorough grounding in the actual scale. B wins narrowly.

criteria.note: Works out 10/s per player and 80/s per server, says each event costs microseconds and a few dozen bytes adding up to a few KB/s, and concludes that none of the items would be noticeable.
Explains that unreliable events drop and reorder messages so a click could quietly do nothing, and adds that `BlockPlacer.start`'s `IsA("RemoteEvent")` assert would fail.

Nothing of the kind is added. The pool is rejected because blocks are never destroyed, the buffer because it saves only a handful of bytes and adds risky decoding of exploiter input, and native code because the scripts mostly call engine APIs and native code has a memory limit.
Removes `VALID_NAMES` and validates with a single `BlockTypes.ByName[blockTypeName]` lookup; all other validation is untouched.
Recommends the MicroProfiler and the Developer Console's Network/Memory tabs, but doesn't specify a server-side capture while players are building.
Only the server script and the doc change, and luau-lsp, selene, and StyLua all pass.
Gives tens of µs per event, well under 1% of a 16.7 ms frame, about 0.3 KB/s per player against budgets of tens of KB/s, and states an explicit rule of not optimizing without a measurement.
Says a dropped `PlaceBlock` is a click that silently places nothing, and notes that reliable events only wait when packets are being lost, which is exactly when an unreliable placement would be lost.

Nothing of the kind is added. Gives concrete reasons: nothing is released to a pool and a reused part keeps the stale `PlacedBy` attribute, a buffer moves validation into hand-written bounds checks, and native code is only supported on some client platforms and draws on a shared memory limit.
Same `ByName` lookup change as A, plus a note that the frozen table has no metatable, so a string like `"__index"` is still rejected.
Recommends a MicroProfiler capture and the Developer Console's network and memory numbers on a live server, and flags total block count as the thing to watch.
Only the server script and the doc change, and all checks pass.

strengths: Clear verdict on each item with a summary table
Catches that the client's `IsA("RemoteEvent")` assert would break under item 3
A sensible cleanup that reuses `ByName` as the single source of truth
weaknesses: The network estimate is less detailed (no per-player rate or budget comparison)

strengths: The most thorough quantification of CPU and network load
Points to the real long-term risk, the unbounded number of blocks, and leaves it as a design decision rather than changing gameplay
Shows that the lookup change keeps behavior identical even for hostile input
weaknesses: Some figures are rough or unsourced (3–6 KB per part, Instance.new vs Clone within 2x)
Misses A's point about the client assert
